extracted.intended_audience: media researchers, journalism students, journalists, and policymakers interested in media quality
extracted.subtask_short: assessing journalistic quality in open societies
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and preconditions for high-quality journalism in democratic/open societies, focusing on three main condition sets (resources, legal/political order, professional standards) and core quality dimensions (independence, diversity, objectivity) with operational implications for empirical assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic quality depends on sufficient resources, including material resources (editorial budgets, technical equipment, subscriptions to news agencies, modern inhouse communication and computing systems) and human capital (availability of talented, well-trained journalists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More money enables more reporters and agency subscriptions, improving diversity and accuracy. Technical infrastructure (internet gateways, external databases) aids reporting. Human capital depends on recruitment mechanisms and educational infrastructure; well-trained journalists are better able to apply norms like objectivity, truth, fairness and neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment openness and professional autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruitment of journalists should be largely unregulated to ensure open access and self-selection into the profession, attracting diverse social groups and highly qualified people; autonomy and opportunities for self-realization make the profession attractive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open access safeguards media diversity; self-selection fosters a heterogeneous profession. Material incentives are less important than autonomy and influence. Investments in journalism education increase quality by equipping journalists to adhere to professional norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and political guarantees for communication freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of laws must guarantee essentials of individual communication freedom: freedom of access to information, freedom of expression, and freedom of distribution of opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic constitutions alone are insufficient—these principles must be transformed into law and judicial practice. Legal guarantees enable independent and objective journalism by protecting the basic freedoms journalists rely on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific legal protections for journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists need specific privileges and protection laws such as a special right of information vis-à-vis state authorities, a right to refuse to give evidence (to protect informants), and protection of editorial offices against confiscation by public prosecutors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These protections help preserve sources and editorial independence; their absence constrains investigative reporting and watchdog functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection from state control and undue influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Media must be protected against state control and against powerful pressure groups or business firms; an absolute ban on state censorship is indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media must not be owned by the state, political parties, or powerful commercial interests (except for internal organizational media). Ownership or board influence undermines impartiality, diversity, and the media's watchdog role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media ownership structure and concentration limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication laws and anti-trust laws must prevent cartels, monopolies and oligopolies in media markets and counteract vertical and diagonal concentration (cross-ownerships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentration reduces media diversity, journalistic competition, and mutual control; regulation should prevent accumulation of media power via cross-ownership and market dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional standards and ethical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic quality depends on the standards and values taken for granted by journalists—routine professional rules (e.g., from BBC Producers' Guidelines): weigh all relevant facts; consider relevant opinions and facts in controversies; admit mistakes clearly and frankly; respect privacy and justify intrusions by a higher public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adherence to these rules distinguishes quality journalism from tabloids/yellow press and commercial media that profit from violations. The norms guide everyday decisions and behavior in borderline situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media self-regulation and enforcement mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions of self-regulation (ombudsman, press council), professional codes of ethics, and professional organizations are necessary to ensure ethical standards are met and to sanction norm violations informally (e.g., loss of reputation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective self-regulation, combined with legal protections (e.g., privacy laws), is important so deviant/tabloid practices are publicly criticized or legally punished; majority adherence to norms and informal sanctions preserve overall media quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of leading quality media
rubrics_metrics.description: A media system should include some leading outlets that set standards: quality newspapers, an intellectual weekly press, and radio/TV stations that comply with social responsibility, public service, and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These leading media influence norms across the system; ensuring they exist helps set benchmarks and promote high-quality performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence (as a core quality criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence comprises two meanings: independence from (state, pressure groups, advertisers, owners) and independence for (ability to advocate and act as a watchdog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both dimensions are essential: independence from undue influence preserves impartiality; independence for advocacy enables critical, watchdog journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity (plurality) of content and access
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity includes (a) diversity of content—opinions, topics, issues, persons/groups, geographic regions—and (b) diversity of access—the forum function ensuring all relevant social groups and political actors can access mass media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two principles for access: equal (open) access (each group receives equal attention in space/time) and proportional (reflective) access (attention proportional to group's importance/size). Access principles are critical during election campaigns when allocation of attention to political parties matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity (decomposed into factuality and impartiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity can be decomposed into factuality and impartiality: factuality further splits into truth and relevance; impartiality includes balance/non-partisanship and neutral presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectivity is philosophically fraught but operationalizable via these concrete subcomponents that tie to everyday journalistic practice (e.g., accurate facts, relevance, balanced coverage, neutral presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factuality: truth and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Factuality requires truthfulness of reported facts and relevance—reporting should focus on information that matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational definitions of truth and relevance are needed for empirical assessment of reporting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality: balance and neutral presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Impartiality requires balance (non-partisanship) and neutral presentation of issues and actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance may mean giving proportional attention or ensuring non-partisan framing; neutral presentation reduces undue framing bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalisability for empirical media-performance research
rubrics_metrics.description: The hierarchical framework should direct development of operational definitions of quality criteria so they can be measured empirically and quantitatively in studies of reporting, programme output, and other media genres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational definitions enable comparative rankings of media and media systems, diagnosing reasons for poor performance and informing policy or reform. The framework supports transforming abstract norms (independence, diversity, objectivity) into measurable indicators.
